Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data

Project Overview

Field Shift is a geospatial agricultural decision-support platform designed to help farmers and agricultural specialists identify which crops are most suitable for a selected area of land.

Agricultural decisions are often made using historical experience and limited local information. However, changing climate conditions, water availability, and differences in environmental characteristics make it increasingly important to understand the specific conditions of each agricultural area.

Field Shift addresses this challenge by combining NASA Earth observation data with agricultural datasets to provide location-specific insights into crop suitability.

How It Works

Users select a geographical area on an interactive map. The platform uses its coordinates to retrieve and analyze relevant environmental information.

The system integrates several data sources:

  • NASA SMAP (Soil Moisture Active Passive): Provides soil moisture observations that help assess water availability and soil moisture conditions.
  • NASA POWER (Prediction Of Worldwide Energy Resources): Provides meteorological and agroclimatic parameters, including temperature, precipitation, and solar radiation.
  • NASA AppEEARS: Enables access to and extraction of supported satellite datasets for the selected geographical area.
  • FAO & IIASA GAEZ (Global Agro-Ecological Zones): Provides agricultural suitability information and crop-specific agroecological requirements.

These datasets are processed and combined within our analytical workflow. The platform evaluates available environmental conditions against the requirements of different crops.

The final output is designed to identify the most suitable crop for the selected area, present a ranked list of alternative crops, and explain the environmental factors influencing the recommendations.

The system also considers data availability and scientific reliability. When information is insufficient to support a reliable assessment, the platform should communicate these limitations rather than generate misleading suitability scores.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Field Shift aims to make agricultural data more accessible and useful for practical decision-making.

Its potential benefits include:

  • Helping farmers make more informed crop-selection decisions.
  • Identifying agricultural opportunities in areas with changing environmental conditions.
  • Supporting more efficient use of agricultural land and available water resources.
  • Providing location-specific insights instead of relying exclusively on general regional recommendations.
  • Supporting climate adaptation through satellite-based environmental monitoring.

Although our initial focus is Uzbekistan, the concept is designed to be applicable to other geographical regions where sufficient environmental and agricultural data are available.

Technology and Development

Field Shift combines geospatial data processing, remote sensing, and agricultural analysis.

The development involves:

  • Python: Data processing and analytical workflows.
  • NASA APIs and data services: Retrieving environmental and satellite information.
  • NASA AppEEARS: Extracting supported Earth observation datasets.
  • GeoTIFF: Working with spatial raster datasets.
  • Geospatial analysis: Processing geographical coordinates and environmental layers.
  • Interactive web mapping: Allowing users to select areas and explore analytical results.
  • FAO GAEZ: Incorporating established agroecological suitability information.

Creativity and Innovation

The main innovative aspect of Field Shift is the integration of satellite-based environmental observations with agricultural suitability assessment in one location-specific platform.

Instead of simply displaying satellite imagery or providing general crop recommendations, Field Shift aims to connect environmental conditions with practical agricultural decisions.

Its modular approach also makes it possible to expand the platform with additional satellite datasets, agricultural indicators, crop types, and geographical regions.

Factors Considered

During development, our team considered several important factors:

  • Climate conditions and seasonal variability.
  • Soil moisture and water availability.
  • Crop-specific environmental requirements.
  • Geographical differences between agricultural areas.
  • Spatial resolution and temporal coverage of satellite datasets.
  • Data quality, uncertainty, and scientific reliability.
  • The need for transparent and explainable recommendations.

Our goal is to turn complex Earth observation data into understandable agricultural insights that can support more informed decisions and help agriculture adapt to a changing planet.
